title: On Trial Until It Proves Itself: A Boot Counter, Rollback by Itself, and Why Confirming at Start-Up Is the Same as Not Checking

questions.question: Why is the try used up before the release runs?
options: So that a release cannot refuse to be tried
A release too broken to say anything must still cost a try: a counter changed only by a working release does not count crashes
Because flash is written before the kernel starts
To keep the count the same on both slots
questions.explanation: If only a working release could decrement the counter, a release that crashes at once would be retried for ever. The boot loader counts, and it is not the thing on trial.

questions.question: A release hangs: up, never healthy, never crashing. What rolls it back?
options: A supervisor that resets the robot at the health deadline: without one it is up for ever doing nothing
The boot counter alone, after three boots
The release's own watchdog thread
Nothing: a hang uses up its tries by itself
questions.explanation: A hang never resets the robot, so the counter never advances. A supervisor that resets it when the health deadline passes turns a hang into a counted failure.

questions.question: A release is healthy at 20 s and crashes at 40 s. It confirms itself when the program starts. What happens?
options: It is rolled back after 4 boots
It runs normally: the crash comes after the confirmation
It confirms again at each boot and stays up
Confirmed at second zero, then crashes with nothing to roll back to: a crash loop, 20 boots and not up
questions.explanation: Confirmed at once, it is no longer on trial when it crashes at 40 s. There is nothing to fall back to, and it looped for all 20 boots.

questions.question: With a crash at 120 s and a healthy time of 20 s, which soaks catch it?
options: All of them: any soak catches a crash
90 s and longer
None: a crash at 120 s is after every soak
100 s and longer: 20 plus the soak must come after the crash, so 90 s is not enough
questions.explanation: Confirmation comes at 20 s plus the soak. With 90 s that is 110 s, before the crash, so the bad release is confirmed. With 100 s the crash comes first.

questions.question: What can the code not know about the soak?
options: Whether it is measured in seconds
How long it takes the failure to show: a leak, a filling disk or a daily task is found from what the robot does
Whether the health checks passed
How many tries the release has left
questions.explanation: The soak has to outlast the time the failure takes to appear. That depends on what the robot does, and has to be found by watching it.

questions.question: Why is a health check not a safety check?
options: A health check runs less often
A safety check is done by the boot loader
A release can be healthy by its own checks and dangerous: the first drive of a new release is with the wheels off the ground
They are the same check under two names
questions.explanation: Healthy means the processes are up and answering. It says nothing about whether the robot will drive into something.
